implementation_notes: The platform ships the pattern: IMemoryCache.GetOrCreate/GetOrCreateAsync hide the miss path, MemoryCacheEntryOptions carries AbsoluteExpirationRelativeToNow, SlidingExpiration, ExpirationTokens, Priority, Size and PostEvictionCallbacks (the invalidation hook), and the default MemoryCache enforces a configured SizeLimit with a compaction percentage. Because the cache is registered in dependency injection (services.AddMemoryCache()), it is injected like any dependency instead of being hidden static state, and IDistributedCache exposes the same entry-option shape over Redis or SQL when the copy must be shared across instances. The hand-written hash-table-plus-recency-list structure is only justified for a single-purpose, allocation-tight store that the framework cache cannot express.
pitfalls: GetOrCreate is not single-flight: concurrent misses of the same key each run the factory, so the provider sees a burst - coalesce the factory or use HybridCache.
Size accounting is all-or-nothing: once SizeLimit is configured, every entry must call SetSize, otherwise insertions fail with InvalidOperationException.
Caching scoped entities (DbContext-bound objects) or request state in the process-wide IMemoryCache keeps them alive after the request and serves stale graphs.
PostEvictionCallbacks run on the eviction path; throwing or blocking inside them interferes with the cache's compaction.

variants.name: HybridCache (ASP.NET Core 9 L1 + L2 with stampede protection)
variants.implementation_notes: HybridCache (ASP.NET Core 9) layers the pattern twice: an in-process L1 IMemoryCache over an optional L2 IDistributedCache, and its single GetOrCreateAsync serializes concurrent misses of the same key so the factory runs once - the stampede protection that plain IMemoryCache lacks. Entries can be tagged for bulk invalidation (RemoveByTagAsync), and options set a factory timeout and separate local/distributed expirations. Choose it when one cache must be both fast locally and shared across instances; without a configured L2 it degenerates to a local cache with extra API surface.
pitfalls: L1 and L2 can disagree: LocalCacheExpiration is per-instance, so a short local expiry plus RemoveByTagAsync is what keeps nodes near-consistent.
Expiration is the only correctness bound for tags on other nodes: tagging without an L2-aware invalidation strategy leaves remote copies alive until they expire.
